title: AgentAM: An AI Agent for Spatter- and Defect-Aware Process Optimization in Laser Powder Bed Fusion
authors: Olabode T. Ajenifujah, Amir Barati Farimani
abstract: Predictive models for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) are rarely used on the shop floor because querying them requires programming and model-specific knowledge. We present AgentAM, a large language model (LLM) agent that gives process engineers natural-language access to CFD-trained surrogates of spatter and melt pool geometry for SS316L through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Polynomial surrogates trained on 279 single-track simulations predict melt pool dimensions ($R^2 \geq 0.95$) and spatter volume ($R^2 = 0.83$ on test data) at any power-velocity point in the trained range, and geometric criteria assign each point a geometry-derived defect regime (keyhole, lack of fusion, balling or stable) that matches the regime obtained from the simulated geometry in 93.4% of tracks under cross-validation. The agent selects and parameterizes tools for prediction, process-window scans and constrained optimization. Minimum-spatter optima often sat within 10 $μ$m of the lack-of-fusion boundary; a margin-aware optimizer moved them away from all thresholds and raised the estimated probability of remaining classified Good from 0.94 to 1.00 under an assumed 2% process drift, and from 0.72 to 0.91 when jointly sampled cross-validated geometry residuals were added. About 40-50 well-spread simulations sufficed to reproduce the defect map. To evaluate the agent layer, we introduce a 145-prompt benchmark scored against direct tool calls, plus eight prompts (40 runs) on margin-aware requests. Over the 725 runs of the main benchmark the agent passed the intended inputs in 98.5% of parsing prompts, reported the scored spatter values and defect classes faithfully and met every stated constraint in the 65 feasible optimization runs, within a median 1.0% of the brute-force optimum.

infographic.key_insight: AgentAM gives engineers natural-language access to LPBF surrogate models, enabling low-spatter process optimization with explicit margins from geometry-derived defect boundaries.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For SS316L, the system could reduce programming barriers to process-window exploration while helping engineers avoid fragile settings near defect thresholds.
method: Connect an LLM agent to CFD-trained polynomial surrogates through the Model Context Protocol.
Predict melt pool geometry and spatter, then classify geometry-derived defect regimes.
Scan power–velocity windows and optimize spatter subject to constraints and defect-boundary margins.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 279 single-track simulations, the surrogates achieved melt pool R² ≥ 0.95 and test spatter R² = 0.83; across 725 agent benchmark runs, all 65 feasible optimization runs met stated constraints, with a median 1.0% gap to the brute-force optimum.
infographic.watch_item: Results are simulation-based and limited to the trained SS316L range; robustness estimates depend on assumed process drift and sampled model residuals, not shop-floor validation.
infographic.paper_title: AgentAM: An AI Agent for Spatter- and Defect-Aware Process Optimization in Laser Powder Bed Fusion

title: Macrocanonical Generator Networks: Data-Efficient Neural Surrogates for Amortized Physics Simulation
authors: Niall Jeffrey, Benjamin D. Wandelt
abstract: Many scientific simulations are computationally expensive, limiting their use in simulation-based inference, uncertainty quantification, and decision making. We introduce macrocanonical generator networks, a framework for learning fast, data-efficient neural surrogates for amortized simulation of stationary physical processes by matching multiscale statistics of a target process. Inspired by microcanonical maximum-entropy synthesis, which matches feature statistics per sample by inner-loop optimization, our approach instead trains a neural generator to satisfy the same constraints in expectation, preserving physically realistic sample-to-sample fluctuations. We prove that gradient-descent training induces preconditioned gradient-descent dynamics in sample space that inherit the symmetry-preservation properties of the microcanonical gradient descent of Bruna and Mallat, amortizing its per-sample inner-loop optimization into a single training run after which every sample is generated in one forward pass. We further show that residual generator parameterizations initialized near the identity, trained with a small learning rate, preserve entropy locally during early optimization and mitigate mode collapse. Experiments on cosmology and fluid simulations show that macrocanonical generators recover realistic samples from extremely small training sets, in some cases a single training example, while generating new realizations more than $10^6$ times faster per sample than the reference simulator and more than $10^3$ times faster than microcanonical gradient descent. The trained generators can be reused for downstream pretraining, including simulation-based inference, providing a data-efficient route to multi-fidelity scientific machine learning workflows.

infographic.key_insight: Macrocanonical generator networks learn fast physics surrogates by matching multiscale statistics in expectation, allowing realistic variation across generated samples.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Once trained, these generators replace costly per-sample simulation or optimization with a single forward pass for uncertainty quantification and simulation-based inference workflows.
method: Train a neural generator to match target multiscale statistics in expectation rather than for each sample.
Amortize symmetry-preserving sample-space optimization into one generator training run.
Use near-identity residual generators and small learning rates to locally preserve entropy early in training and mitigate mode collapse.
infographic.evidence_signal: Cosmology and fluid experiments report realistic samples from very small training sets, sometimes one example, with per-sample generation over 10^6 times faster than reference simulators and over 10^3 times faster than microcanonical gradient descent.
infographic.watch_item: Matching selected statistics does not by itself establish accuracy for every downstream observable; validate task-specific behavior before replacing a simulator.
infographic.paper_title: Macrocanonical Generator Networks: Data-Efficient Neural Surrogates for Amortized Physics Simulation

title: Multi-Objective Generative Optimization via Expected Hypervolume Fine-Tuning
authors: Juan Guevara, Riccardo De Santi, Andreas Krause, Raul Astudillo
abstract: Scientific discovery requires plausible designs spanning useful trade-offs among competing properties: a molecule with strong binding affinity, for example, may be difficult to synthesize. Pretrained generative models, e.g., flow and diffusion generators, provide a foundation for proposing such designs, but steering them toward high-quality, complementary trade-offs remains challenging. Inference-time search incurs high per-sample costs, while fine-tuning typically relies on fixed per-candidate rewards that do not capture how designs complement one another. We introduce Hypervolume Fine-Tuning (HVFT), which adapts a single pretrained generator to maximize the expected hypervolume of its samples while controlling departure from the pretrained distribution. Expected hypervolume jointly rewards candidate quality and collective trade-off coverage. Nonetheless, we show that it cannot be expressed as the expectation of a fixed per-candidate reward and therefore cannot be optimized directly with standard techniques. A key observation of this work is that its first variation corresponds to the expected marginal hypervolume contribution of a candidate, which yields a tractable adaptive reward via an unbiased estimator based on model samples. HVFT uses this reward to decompose the objective into a sequence of KL-proximal scalar-reward subproblems. We establish concavity, relative smoothness, and convergence guarantees for the resulting distributional procedure. Across therapeutic-peptide and molecular design tasks spanning discrete diffusion and continuous flow-matching models, HVFT achieves state-of-the-art expected hypervolume and trade-off coverage.

infographic.key_insight: Hypervolume Fine-Tuning (HVFT) steers a pretrained generator toward sets of designs that jointly improve quality and cover complementary trade-offs among competing objectives.
infographic.engineering_relevance: HVFT offers a way to adapt generative design pipelines for multi-objective discovery without relying on fixed per-candidate rewards or costly inference-time search.
method: Maximize expected sample-set hypervolume while controlling departure from the pretrained distribution.
Estimate adaptive rewards from each candidate’s expected marginal hypervolume contribution using model samples.
Optimize successive KL-proximal scalar-reward subproblems, with distributional convergence guarantees.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art expected hypervolume and trade-off coverage on therapeutic-peptide and molecular design tasks using discrete diffusion and continuous flow-matching models.
infographic.watch_item: Practical training cost and stability require scrutiny because adaptive rewards depend on model sampling and marginal hypervolume estimation.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-Objective Generative Optimization via Expected Hypervolume Fine-Tuning

title: Catalyzing Interactive HTML Generation Capabilities via High-Fidelity Reinforcement Learning
authors: Xujia Wang, Yixuan Liu, Shaohan Huang, Furu Wei, Lei Hou, Bin Xu
abstract: Generating HTML from natural-language specifications is an important application of code large language models (LLMs). Despite producing renderable pages, current models often fail to ensure functionality and visual quality during actual interaction. Existing methods typically target task-specific webpage supervision, leaving demanding interactive artifact optimization underexplored. Using mini-games as a challenging testbed, we expose limitations in interaction experience, reward signal, and credit assignment fidelity that are obscured by shallow webpage interactions. We introduce WebCatalyst, a browser-interaction reinforcement learning framework with three complementary components: a game-level GUI assessor for sustained interaction and evaluation, Visual Anchor for mitigating VLM reward hacking, and Action-Trace Credit for grounding token-level credit assignment in runtime execution traces. Trained on fewer than 1K requests, predominantly for games, WebCatalyst raises the Cookie-Bench Mini Games score from 68.8 to 75.3 and also the WebGen-Bench accuracy from 48.8 to 56.9 on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, outperforming Claude Opus 4.7 in average rank across evaluated metrics. Further analysis shows that Visual Anchor prevents aesthetic degradation, while runtime-grounded credit assignment accelerates functional improvement. Together, our results show that improving feedback fidelity is the key to substantially advancing interactive HTML generation.

infographic.key_insight: WebCatalyst improves interactive HTML generation by making reinforcement-learning feedback more faithful to sustained browser interaction, visual quality, and runtime behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a way to optimize generated web artifacts for actual usability and appearance rather than renderability alone.
method: Use a game-level GUI assessor for sustained browser interaction and evaluation.
Apply Visual Anchor to mitigate vision-language-model reward hacking and aesthetic degradation.
Use Action-Trace Credit to ground token-level credit assignment in runtime execution traces.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on fewer than 1,000 mostly game requests raised Cookie-Bench Mini Games scores from 68.8 to 75.3 and WebGen-Bench accuracy from 48.8 to 56.9.
infographic.watch_item: The game-heavy training and evaluation focus leaves generalization to broader, production-grade web interactions uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Catalyzing Interactive HTML Generation Capabilities via High-Fidelity Reinforcement Learning

title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents
authors: Hongyin Luo, Wei Fang, Lijie Yang, Owen Stepan, Daniel Suit, Jeff Krapf
abstract: Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.

infographic.key_insight: Training a speculative draft model to trigger rejection at critical reasoning points can improve long-horizon agent accuracy by restarting target-model verification under lower-noise conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Speculative decoding may serve as a precision-allocation mechanism for coding agents, not just a speed optimization, without modifying the target model.
method: Identify critical decision points in agent reasoning traces.
Train the draft model to favor alternatives that the target model rejects at those points.
Restart verification so critical tokens receive lower-noise target-model processing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports higher end-to-end success on complex agentic coding benchmarks using frontier open-weight models while training 0.06%–0.28% of hosted parameters, but provides no numerical success gains.
infographic.watch_item: Deliberately increasing rejection could reduce decoding efficiency; the abstract does not quantify the latency trade-off.
infographic.paper_title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents

title: JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks
authors: Shanka Subhra Mondal, Jiayun Wang
abstract: Multimodal web agents have shown promising capabilities for interacting with websites through graphical user interfaces (GUIs), yet realistic web tasks often require long-horizon, multi-step planning that remains challenging for monolithic policies. Such agents must jointly infer high-level plans, navigate through intermediate states, track progress over extended interaction histories, and execute visually grounded actions. Although prior work has explored modular multi-agent systems with a separate planner, the planner is typically not updated jointly with the actor. We investigate whether explicitly separating and jointly training planning and execution provides a stronger inductive bias for long-horizon web navigation. We introduce JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for web agents that couples a task decomposer with an actor. To train the decomposer, we use a strong teacher model to construct structured subtask supervision from multimodal GUI trajectories, and use these annotations to fine-tune both the decomposer and the subtask-conditioned actor. We then extend Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to jointly optimize the decomposer and actor in the interactive WebArena environment through hierarchical rollout grouping and role-specific advantages. On WebArena-Lite-v2, JHiMA-WebRL-14B, consisting of a 7B actor and a 7B decomposer, achieves an average success rate of 37.2%, compared with 24% for a ScaleCUA-32B agent that we fine-tune with RL on the same training tasks and evaluate under the same protocol. Ablations show that jointly updating the decomposer during RL outperforms updating the actor alone. These results suggest that jointly learned role factorization with smaller models can be a competitive alternative to scaling monolithic agents for long-horizon web tasks.

infographic.key_insight: Jointly training separate planning and execution agents improves long-horizon web task success over a larger monolithic agent in the reported evaluation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Role-specialized smaller models offer a promising alternative to scaling a single model for complex GUI automation.
method: Separate task decomposition from subtask-conditioned action execution.
Fine-tune both agents using teacher-generated subtask annotations from multimodal GUI trajectories.
Jointly optimize both agents with hierarchical rollout grouping and role-specific GRPO advantages.
infographic.evidence_signal: On WebArena-Lite-v2, the 7B decomposer plus 7B actor achieved 37.2% average success versus 24% for an RL-fine-tuned ScaleCUA-32B under the same protocol; ablations favored joint updates over actor-only updates.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond WebArena-Lite-v2 and the inference cost of coordinating two agents remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks

title: Learning curves in natural and artificial systems
authors: Dmitry A. Novikov
abstract: A general mathematical model of experience formation is considered, in which the learning level is defined as the probability that the next value of the uncertainty factor has already been mastered and not forgotten. Within this model the shape of the learning curve is derived, and it turns out to be determined primarily by the distribution of situation occurrence: a uniform distribution yields an exponential curve, whereas a power-law distribution yields a power-law curve whose exponent equals the ratio of the distribution exponent to that same exponent increased by one. Both mechanisms generating power-law curves, established earlier in the analysis of debugging, assembly and repair activities, are shown to have been independently rediscovered in deep learning theory as the "frequency" and "spectral" mechanisms of scaling laws for artificial neural networks, while the exponential curves of machine learning (contraction operators, strongly convex optimization, stationary reinforcement) are generated by the same constancy of the contraction coefficient that was revealed half a century earlier in models of radioactive decay, the first-order lag element, and others. A solution is given for the problem of choosing a training distribution that differs from the deployment distribution. A methodological consequence is discussed: three distinct mechanisms generate curves indistinguishable in shape, so an observed learning curve does not allow one to judge the "internal" structure of the learning system.

infographic.key_insight: Learning-curve shape depends primarily on how situations occur: uniform occurrence yields exponential learning, while power-law occurrence yields power-law learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects learning laws across natural and artificial systems and addresses choosing a training distribution that differs from deployment.
method: Define learning level as the probability that the next situation has been mastered and not forgotten.
Derive learning curves from situation-occurrence distributions.
Relate power-law and exponential mechanisms to neural scaling laws and constant-contraction processes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports mathematical derivations and cross-domain theoretical connections, but no empirical datasets, benchmarks, or quantitative validation.
infographic.watch_item: Different mechanisms can produce indistinguishable learning curves, so curve shape alone cannot identify a system’s internal learning structure.
infographic.paper_title: Learning curves in natural and artificial systems

title: A Bayesian Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg Model for Real-Time EEG Phase Estimation
authors: Ivan Martinez-Kay, Tatiana Kardashina, ShiNung Ching, Eric C. Leuthardt, Benjamin T. Acland
abstract: Real-time phase estimation on stimulus-aligned transient EEG is critical for closed-loop neuromodulation systems targeting the theta-band, yet most real-time phase estimation methods have been developed and validated on resting-state, high-fidelity signals in the alpha band. Recent work has pursued deep learning architectures, while individualized classical bandpass filter tuning remains underexplored. This study characterizes the spectral and temporal properties of non-anticipative bandpass filtering and demonstrates the performance gains achieved through individualized tuning. We present a Bayesian-Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg (BOB) model evaluated on EEG recorded during peripheral vibrotactile stimulation of the left median nerve (theta, N=20 healthy subjects) and on resting-state recordings from the Max Planck Institute's LEMON dataset (alpha, N=20 healthy subjects). BOB was benchmarked against the Deep Dual-Branch Complex Neural Network (DBCNN), EEG Phase Prediction Network (EPN), Phastimate, and Phase Estimation with Autoregressive Padding (PEAP) under matched testing conditions: channel selection, individualized optimization, evaluation time points, and an offline reference phase obtained through zero-phase filtering and the Hilbert transform. Under these testing conditions, BOB achieved matched or better performance than these models at a fraction of the calibration time.

infographic.key_insight: Individualized Bayesian tuning of a classical Biquad Filter-Burg model matched or outperformed neural and classical EEG phase estimators with substantially less calibration time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: BOB offers a calibration-efficient approach to real-time EEG phase estimation for closed-loop neuromodulation, including stimulus-aligned theta activity.
method: Characterize spectral and temporal properties of non-anticipative bandpass filtering.
Use Bayesian optimization to individualize the Biquad Filter-Burg phase estimator.
Benchmark against DBCNN, EPN, Phastimate, and PEAP under matched testing conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation used stimulation-evoked theta EEG from 20 healthy subjects and resting-state alpha EEG from 20 LEMON participants, with matched channel selection, individualized optimization, evaluation times, and an offline zero-phase-filter/Hilbert reference.
infographic.watch_item: Results in healthy-subject recordings do not establish performance in clinical populations or deployed closed-loop systems.
infographic.paper_title: A Bayesian Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg Model for Real-Time EEG Phase Estimation

title: Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization
authors: Austin Tsai, Saurav Nanda, Ganapathy Parthasarathy, Bhuvnesh Kumar, Parivesh Choudhary
abstract: Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game. Its practical variant, DNO-Prct, iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of the samples together with a teacher's gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection and a DPO-style contrastive update. We re-implement DNO-Prct independently and study it on two open-weight instruct models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1, with GPT-4o or a larger open-weight model of the same family as the annotator. On AlpacaEval 2.0 with GPT-4o as judge, three iterations raise the length-controlled (LC) win rate against GPT-4o from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama and from 6.8% to 18.4% for Mistral, and the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on every reported win rate. With same-family open-weight annotators, the runs retain 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain achieved with GPT-4o as annotator, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model. In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or accept only teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure, whereas varying the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points. We also report the cost of the pipeline and where the practical algorithm departs from the theory it approximates. All results are single runs, and GPT-4o is both the teacher and the evaluation judge; we discuss what this implies for the reported gains.

infographic.key_insight: Three iterations of practical Direct Nash Optimization improved length-controlled win rates against GPT-4o from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama 3.1 8B and from 6.8% to 18.4% for Mistral 7B.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Same-family open-weight annotators retained 62% of Llama’s and 82% of Mistral’s gains achieved with GPT-4o annotation, offering a nonproprietary option for the rating step.
method: Sample responses on-policy and rate them alongside a teacher’s gold response.
Select large-margin preference pairs and apply a DPO-style contrastive update.
Repeat training to approximate a two-player preference-game Nash equilibrium.
infographic.evidence_signal: On AlpacaEval 2.0 with GPT-4o judging, the tuned Llama 3.1 8B exceeded Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on every reported win-rate metric.
infographic.watch_item: All results are single runs, and using GPT-4o as both teacher and evaluation judge may favor alignment to that model’s preferences.
infographic.paper_title: Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization

title: De Rham cohomological architectures for PINNs and PDEs with topological holes
authors: Andrew Gracyk
abstract: We attempt to alleviate failure modes of classical physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in scenarios of topological pathologies corresponding to punctures, holes, poles, and voids by introducing de Rham cohomological augmentations, or Hodge-de Rham PINNs. Vanilla PINNs often encounter pitfalls in hole-based settings due to discontinuous interfaces, nonzero closed path integration, path dependence, correspondence to exact forms via the exterior derivative, etc., therefore we absolve traditional failures via parameterizing a 1-form by the Hodge-Morrey-Friedrichs (HMF) decomposition for manifolds with boundary, drawing a connection to de Rham cohomology such as through the HMF isomorphism theorem. 1-forms can act as representations of scalar-valued PDE solutions through integral operator mappings. We propose performing a PINN-based loss on the parameterized 1-form through an associated PDE, which subsequently solves the potential-based PINN problem and moreover remedies the failures of vanilla PINNs via the Sobolev-regular operator under a Fréchet differentiation interconnection. The operator relationship often has a nontrivial closed-form and often requires integration or a case-by-case analysis, which we address thoroughly in our experiments. When an integrability condition is not met on our losses, we can equip exhaustion functions to train the networks. We demonstrate our methods on the Aharonov-Bohm effect, which, to our understanding, is largely nonexistent in PINN literature. We develop theoretical guarantees of our methods and demonstrate our pathological safeguards on a broad selection of topologically-adverse problems, including scenarios of inexact forms, and those of nontrivial harmonics and coexact terms.

infographic.key_insight: Hodge–de Rham PINNs augment neural PDE solvers with topology-aware 1-forms to address failures caused by holes, punctures, and nontrivial circulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could improve physics-informed modeling on multiply connected domains where a globally defined scalar potential cannot capture essential solution structure.
method: Parameterize a 1-form using the Hodge–Morrey–Friedrichs decomposition for manifolds with boundary.
Train with an associated PDE loss and connect the learned form to scalar solutions through integral operators.
Use exhaustion functions when the loss integrability condition is not satisfied.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees and experiments on topologically adverse problems, including the Aharonov–Bohm effect, but provides no quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The operator linking 1-forms to scalar solutions may require integration or problem-specific derivation, complicating implementation.
infographic.paper_title: De Rham cohomological architectures for PINNs and PDEs with topological holes

title: iGC: Antibody Optimization via Reinforcement Learning over a Learned Somatic Hypermutation Prior
authors: Thao Nguyen, Robert G. Alberstein, Ewa Nowara, Homa MohammadiPeyhani, Holly R. Steach, Sarah A. Robinson
abstract: Antibody affinity maturation is a natural optimization process in which B cells acquire mutations through somatic hypermutation (SHM), undergo selection for improved antigen binding, and iteratively evolve toward higher affinity. Computationally modeling this process requires capturing both biologically plausible mutations and antigen-specific selection. However, existing mutation models do not directly optimize binding, while affinity optimization often neglects realistic mutation trajectories. We introduce iGC (in silico Germinal Centers), a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) framework for antigen-specific antibody optimization. Stage 1 learns an SHM mutation prior from parent-child pairs in B-cell lineage trees and adapts it to a target affinity-maturation dataset. Stage 2 initializes an RL policy from this prior and optimizes antigen binding with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization toward the frozen prior. To prevent reward exploitation, including repetitive high-reward substitutions and structurally tolerated framework mutations, we introduce a Reward-Tax Meta-Gradient objective. RewardNet smooths the affinity landscape, while TaxNet penalizes reward overexploitation, jointly defining a learned meta-reward for policy optimization. We evaluate iGC on mutation prediction, SHM consistency, affinity optimization, and mutation diversity. The mutation prior more than doubles the strongest baseline in mutation-site prediction. Following RL optimization, iGC maintains SHM sequence structure. It also achieves a strong exploration-exploitation balance, yielding competitive reward-diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs. These results demonstrate that iGC integrates biologically plausible mutation generation with antigen-specific affinity selection, providing an in silico framework for iterative antibody affinity maturation.

infographic.key_insight: iGC combines a learned somatic hypermutation prior with reinforcement learning to optimize antibody binding while preserving biologically plausible mutation patterns.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a strategy for antibody candidate generation that balances predicted binding improvement, mutation realism, and sequence diversity.
method: Learn a mutation prior from parent–child B-cell lineage pairs, then adapt it to a target affinity-maturation dataset.
Initialize an RL policy from the prior and optimize antigen binding with KL regularization toward the frozen prior.
Use RewardNet and TaxNet in a meta-gradient objective to smooth affinity rewards and penalize reward exploitation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports more than twice the strongest baseline's mutation-site prediction performance, retained SHM sequence structure after RL, and competitive reward–diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report experimental binding validation, so predicted affinity gains require laboratory confirmation.
infographic.paper_title: iGC: Antibody Optimization via Reinforcement Learning over a Learned Somatic Hypermutation Prior

title: OperAItor: An Agentic Framework for Fault-Tolerant Operation of Chemical Processes
authors: Javal Vyas, Mehmet Mercang{ö}z
abstract: OperAItor, an open-source framework for developing and evaluating large language model agents for supervisory fault management in chemical processes. The framework is demonstrated on a dynamic reactor-distillation process representing isopropanol dehydrogenation, with physically based thermodynamics and modified reaction kinetics to permit liquid-phase operation. The process is represented by a 113-variable differential-algebraic model and operates at a nominal feed rate of 100kmol/h, producing approximately 4t/h of acetone. The simulated plant includes 8 PI control loops, 22 process alarms, 5 duty-standby pump trains, and 11 independent safety instrumented functions. The agent architecture integrates multivariate statistical process monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval, action planning, and supervisory action generation. Five action-validation configurations are investigated, comprising operation without validation, an LLM-based judge, digital-twin simulation, and deterministic admissibility checks with and without consequence projection. The framework is evaluated using four LLMs across 20 scenarios involving single and multiple simultaneous faults. Without agent intervention, 18 scenarios result in plant stops, corresponding to an economic loss of $399,000 relative to fault-free operation under the assumed benchmark economics. For GPT-5 nano, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, validated agent configurations reduce the number of stops to 5-8 and recover $265,000 of the loss. The study provides a reproducible benchmark for comparing agent architectures, language models, and action-validation methods for supervisory fault management in chemical processes.

infographic.key_insight: OperAItor combines LLM agents with process monitoring and action validation to reduce simulated chemical-plant shutdowns during faults.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The open-source framework offers a reproducible benchmark for supervisory fault management above conventional process controls and safety systems.
method: Integrate statistical monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval, and action planning.
Compare five action-validation configurations, including no validation, an LLM judge, digital-twin simulation, and deterministic checks.
Test four LLMs on a 113-variable reactor–distillation model across 20 fault scenarios.
infographic.evidence_signal: Without intervention, 18 of 20 scenarios stopped the simulated plant; validated configurations using GPT-5 nano, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B reduced stops to 5–8 and recovered $265,000 under benchmark economics.
infographic.watch_item: Results are simulation-based; deployment requires validation against real plant dynamics, safety constraints, and operating economics.
infographic.paper_title: OperAItor: An Agentic Framework for Fault-Tolerant Operation of Chemical Processes

title: Meta$^2$: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents
authors: Lingzhi Yuan, Yiguang Cai, Weize Liu, Siqi Yang, Feijiang Han, Yongkyun Lee
abstract: Harness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online evolution can adapt before, during, or after one run through an evolver, but may have to reason about every intervention from scratch or rely on verifier feedback that is usually unavailable at test time. We introduce Meta$^2$, which moves offline optimization one level up: rather than optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable knowledge for harness evolution and applies it within each task online. Offline, Meta$^2$ learns a textual Meta-Skill $M$ by contrasting training rollouts of the same task agent under three configurations: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current version of $M$, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only in training. Contrasts in trajectories and outcomes are aggregated across tasks to refine $M$ into reusable guidance on when and how to evolve, when to leave the harness unchanged, and which interventions to avoid. Online, an evolver combines the frozen $M$ with emerging trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness unchanged or EVOLVE it through a task-local edit. Each edit applies to the rest of the same run without resetting its environment or progress. Thus, evolution guidance transfers across tasks while harness edits remain task-local, and held-out verifier feedback is never available to the evolver. On two long-horizon benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1, Meta$^2$ achieves the highest performance among evaluated methods with GPT-5.6-Terra, reaching 81.00% and 44.44%, respectively. Ablations support the value of contrastive evolution guidance and keeping online harness edits task-local.

infographic.key_insight: Meta² learns reusable guidance offline so an online evolver can adapt a frozen-model agent’s harness to each task without test-time verifier feedback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Long-horizon agents can adjust prompts, tools, memory, and hooks during execution while preserving environment state and task progress.
method: Contrast training rollouts with no evolver, a Meta-Skill-guided evolver, and an evolver given training-only privileged verifier information.
Aggregate trajectory and outcome differences into a textual Meta-Skill describing when to intervene, when to keep the harness unchanged, and which edits to avoid.
Freeze the Meta-Skill online; use emerging evidence to choose KEEP or EVOLVE, with edits confined to the current run.
infographic.evidence_signal: With GPT-5.6-Terra, Meta² achieved the highest performance among evaluated methods on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (81.00%) and DeepSWE 1.1 (44.44%); ablations supported contrastive guidance and task-local edits.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover two benchmarks with one reported model, leaving broader transfer and online intervention overhead uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Meta$^2$: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents

title: Agnostic Learning by Imitating
authors: Sílvia Casacuberta, Parikshit Gopalan, Varun Kanade, Omer Reingold, Konstantinos Stavropoulos, Pranay Tankala
abstract: Given a class of machine learning models and sample access to a data distribution with binary labels, which computational task is harder: training a discriminative model that distinguishes positive and negative labels as well as the best member of the class, or training a generative model whose outputs are indistinguishable from real data by all members of the class? We prove that these two fundamental tasks in computational learning theory are not just closely related, but actually equivalent to each other in complexity. One direction of this equivalence was previously known. Indeed, the powerful regularity lemma in complexity theory gives an efficient oracle reduction from the indistinguishability task (a.k.a. multiaccuracy) to the distinguishing task (a.k.a. agnostic learning) in the style of boosting algorithms. Our main contribution is an efficient oracle reduction in the other direction. Taking this idea further, we show that a multiaccuracy oracle is a remarkably powerful primitive, achieving not just agnostic learning but also a wide range of seemingly more demanding learning objectives via similarly efficient and direct constructions. Our results crucially use the power of making adaptive queries to the oracle, and stand in stark contrast to prior work, which showed that post-processing a single multiaccurate predictor is insufficient for even weak forms of learning. On a technical level, we draw a connection between our (offline) problem and a version of no-regret learning in the online setting, which allows us to use follow-the-leader type algorithms to modify the label distribution and aggregate the predictions of the multiaccuracy oracle.

infographic.key_insight: Agnostic learning and generating outputs indistinguishable from real data by a model class are computationally equivalent via efficient oracle reductions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result identifies multiaccuracy as a reusable theoretical primitive for agnostic learning and broader learning objectives.
method: Prove the previously missing reduction from agnostic learning to a multiaccuracy oracle.
Make adaptive oracle queries while modifying the label distribution and aggregating predictions.
Use a connection to online no-regret learning and follow-the-leader algorithms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical proofs of efficient reductions, not empirical datasets or benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: The constructions require adaptive oracle access; post-processing a single multiaccurate predictor is insufficient even for weak forms of learning.
infographic.paper_title: Agnostic Learning by Imitating

title: Molecular Prior Networks
authors: Pawel Gomoluch, Anthony Bradley
abstract: Predicting affinity between small molecules and their protein targets remains one of the central problems in drug discovery. Due to the substantial cost of wet-lab experiments, machine learning models of drug-target affinity are usually trained on relatively small datasets, ranging from tens to hundreds of molecules. Given the inherent difficulty of generalization between different targets and chemical series, existing datasets of protein-ligand affinities are typically not used for new projects. At the same time, tabular foundation models, including Prior-data Fitted Networks, have recently shown how transformers can be used to solve machine learning problems in a single forward pass of the network, after being trained over a large corpus of, typically, synthetic datasets. Inspired by that line of work, we propose a novel affinity modelling approach, in which the labels of the query molecules are predicted from the labelled support molecules in a single forward pass of a transformer model. The model is trained on thousands of existing affinity datasets, enabling it to capture the general patterns of molecular activity across different targets, chemical series and dataset sizes. For the smallest support sets, our model matches the state of the art on the regression variant of the FS-Mol benchmark, while being faster than existing methods, thanks to the lack of task-specific training. A comparison against a reduced variant of our architecture, which amounts to kernel regression in a meta-learned feature space, shows that the predictive performance of the transformer model is only partially explained by simple molecular similarity.

infographic.key_insight: Molecular Prior Networks predict drug–target affinity from labelled support molecules in a single transformer forward pass, without task-specific training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can accelerate low-data affinity modelling for drug discovery by reusing patterns learned across existing affinity datasets.
method: Train a transformer on thousands of existing molecular affinity datasets.
Condition query predictions on labelled support molecules.
Compare against kernel regression in a meta-learned feature space to probe the role of molecular similarity.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the regression variant of FS-Mol, the model matches state-of-the-art performance for the smallest support sets while running faster than existing methods.
infographic.watch_item: The reported state-of-the-art match is limited to the smallest support sets; broader performance across dataset sizes and novel targets requires verification.
infographic.paper_title: Molecular Prior Networks

title: Beyond Foundation Models: PFN Priors Improve Tabular Hyperparameter Optimization
authors: Artem Chistyakov, Renat Sergazinov, Artem Babenko
abstract: Synthetic priors have so far served one purpose: pretraining tabular foundation models. We ask whether the same priors can improve conventional tabular models, which are trained from scratch on each dataset. We propose PriorTune, a method that meta-tunes hyperparameter configurations on synthetic tasks alone. Offline, for a given model, we fit a pool of configurations on datasets sampled from a published PFN prior and greedily select the subset with the highest winrate over the random baseline. Online, a new dataset fits only the selected configurations, so the gain comes at no extra cost. Empirically, we observe that scaling both the number of configurations and synthetic datasets has an equal scaling effect on the performance of the final subset of configurations, which we also explain theoretically. On the full BeyondArena benchmark, LightGBM with TabPrep features with our configurations ranks above TabPFN-3 and RealMLP, while being much more efficient at inference. Overall, our results establish existing PFN priors as a scalable source of meta-training data for hyperparameter selection for non-foundational tabular models.

infographic.key_insight: PriorTune uses synthetic PFN-prior tasks to select hyperparameter configurations that improve conventional tabular models without increasing online search cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Teams can move hyperparameter selection offline, then evaluate a preselected configuration set on new datasets for efficient tabular modeling.
method: Train a pool of model configurations on synthetic datasets sampled from a published PFN prior.
Greedily select configurations to maximize win rate against a random baseline.
On each new dataset, fit only the selected configurations.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the full BeyondArena benchmark, LightGBM with TabPrep features and PriorTune configurations ranks above TabPFN-3 and RealMLP while offering much more efficient inference.
infographic.watch_item: Offline meta-tuning requires substantial configuration evaluations, and transfer to new domains may depend on how well the synthetic prior represents them.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Foundation Models: PFN Priors Improve Tabular Hyperparameter Optimization

title: Towards an Optimal Control Foundation of Early Exits - Turnpikes and ResNets
authors: Jens Püttschneider, Simon Heilig, Asja Fischer, Timm Faulwasser
abstract: The feed-forward propagation through neural networks is crucial for training and inference. To trade off efficiency and accuracy, it has been proposed to consider intermediate outputs of hidden states as data-dependent regularization during training and, ultimately, as early-exits during inference. In this work, we analyze the joint optimization of loss functions computed for the output layer and intermediate layers using optimal control theory. We prove that ResNets trained in this joint fashion exhibit the so-called turnpike phenomenon, this implies that the number of layers required to reach a prescribed loss level is bounded from above independently of the overall network depth. This induces a similarity property across the internal representations of early-exiting networks of varying depths. We connect the turnpike to the overthinking phenomenon, and provide theoretical insights into the success of early-exit criteria derived from softmax probabilities, specifically entropy and max-probability. In a range of experiments, we demonstrate the existence and effect of turnpikes and the resulting similarity in the early-exit performance for ResNets of varying depths.

infographic.key_insight: For jointly supervised ResNets, the authors prove a turnpike property: the number of layers needed to reach a prescribed loss level is bounded independently of total network depth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory helps explain why early exits can reduce inference computation and why networks of different depths can show similar early-exit performance.
method: Model ResNet propagation and joint intermediate/output loss optimization using optimal control theory.
Prove a turnpike property and derive similarity implications for internal representations across network depths.
Connect turnpikes to overthinking and analyze entropy- and maximum-probability-based exit criteria.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments demonstrate turnpike behavior and similar early-exit performance across ResNets of varying depths; the abstract provides no datasets or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify the theorem’s assumptions, so its depth-independent guarantee should not be assumed to cover arbitrary architectures or training setups.
infographic.paper_title: Towards an Optimal Control Foundation of Early Exits - Turnpikes and ResNets

title: Shrinkage prior for implicit generative models
authors: Shreya Sinha-Roy, Christian P. Robert, Ritabrata Dutta
abstract: Implicit generative models based on deep neural networks have revolutionized many scientific fields, from weather research to language generation. They successfully model complex random objects arising in real-world problems. In this work, we propose a sample-efficient training mechanism for these models. Our approach leverages regularized inference with shrinkage priors and generalized Bayes. In the large $p$ (parameter dimension) and small $n$ (sample size) setting, sparsity-inducing priors have been successfully used for linear regression when $p \gg n$. However, their application to implicit generative models remains challenging due to the intractability of the likelihood function. To address this, we adapt a scoring rule posterior based on a strictly proper scoring rule, following the generalized Bayes framework. We then propose a block SGMCMC within Gibbs sampling mechanism. This enables efficient exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces by identifying a sparse representation of neural implicit generative models. We demonstrate the performance of our proposed method through experiments on $p \gg n$ linear regression and an application of neural generative models.

infographic.key_insight: Shrinkage priors combined with generalized Bayes offer a sample-efficient way to train neural implicit generative models by promoting sparse parameter representations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets data-limited settings where neural model parameter counts greatly exceed available training samples.
method: Replace the intractable likelihood with a posterior based on a strictly proper scoring rule.
Apply sparsity-inducing shrinkage priors to regularize model parameters.
Use block stochastic-gradient MCMC within Gibbs sampling to explore the high-dimensional posterior.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experiments on linear regression with far more parameters than samples and an application to neural generative models, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: High-dimensional posterior sampling requires careful convergence checks; the abstract does not establish computational cost or scalability.
infographic.paper_title: Shrinkage prior for implicit generative models

title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
authors: Kewei Zhang, Juncheng Ma, Guodong Lv, Duomin Wang, Feixiang Ruan, Ruiyang Si
abstract: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs \$21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus \$5 for a render contract; every further episode costs \$0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs \$107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of \$117 for teleoperation in China and below \$290 in labour alone in North America.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM coding agent can turn one real calibration episode into action-labelled, multiview robot training data that supports direct deployment on real hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach reduces repeated robot and operator use, with reported costs of $107 per hour of three-view data versus quoted teleoperation costs of $117 in China and $290 in North American labour alone.
method: Given a data request and calibration episode, the agent builds a simulated scene, expert controller, and success judge.
Simulation supplies exact actions; a real-image-conditioned video model renders synchronized, consistent camera views.
Independent judges check the expert and each rendered episode before admitting data for policy training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five real-robot tasks, farm-trained policies achieved 93/100 successes versus 84/100 for teleoperation-trained policies; under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light, they achieved 87 versus 46.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence covers only five tasks; broader deployment requires validating rendering fidelity and automated judges on new scenes and robot behaviours.
infographic.paper_title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data

title: Creating Power Flexibility in Datacenters via Query Routing
authors: Shivam Patel, Bingqing Chen, Jared Fernandez, Guannan Qu, Gauri Joshi
abstract: The growing energy requirements of large language model inference highlight the need for datacenters to support safe grid operation by providing power demand flexibility, while maintaining service for interactive workloads. This work investigates query routing as a mechanism to enable such capability by dynamically allocating queries across different language model instances without deferring requests. We develop a general analytical framework that connects query arrival rates and sequence length distributions to token iteration time, request residence time, serving capacity, and power consumption of model instances. Leveraging this framework, we characterize the feasible query routing allocations and the corresponding power demand flexibilities, enabling the selection of routing strategies to achieve desired power consumption behavior. We validate our framework across four GPU platforms on language models ranging from 1B to 70B parameters, obtaining 2.8% mean absolute percentage error in estimating achievable power flexibility. We evaluate our approach on a real trace-driven simulation of a 10,000 H100 GPUs datacenter, exhibiting flexibility up to 16% of total power consumption, with 90% of the desired power reduction achieved within approximately 10 seconds. These results establish query routing as an effective mechanism for datacenter power demand flexibility and demonstrate the broader applicability of our proposed framework to datacenter level planning and orchestration.

infographic.key_insight: Dynamically routing queries across language model instances can adjust datacenter power demand without deferring requests.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Query routing offers a software-level mechanism for grid-responsive power management while maintaining service for interactive workloads.
method: Model how query arrival rates and sequence lengths affect token iteration time, request residence time, serving capacity, and power.
Characterize feasible routing allocations and their achievable power flexibility.
Select routing strategies to achieve desired power consumption behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation across four GPU platforms and 1B–70B models yielded 2.8% mean absolute percentage error in estimated flexibility; a trace-driven simulation of 10,000 H100 GPUs showed up to 16% power flexibility, achieving 90% of the desired reduction in approximately 10 seconds.
infographic.watch_item: Datacenter-scale results are simulation-based; production deployment should verify response times and interactive service performance under changing workloads.
infographic.paper_title: Creating Power Flexibility in Datacenters via Query Routing
